passA.summary: Veronica Hylak argues that most AI products fail not because the technology is weak but because nobody can explain them, and offers a three-part storytelling method for fixing that. Step one is to open with 'the wound' — the customer's concrete daily pain — rather than with what you built. Step two is to make the product click by anchoring it to an image or viral story a 17-year-old would instantly grasp, deferring precise technical definitions until later in the sale. Step three is to show a before/after transformation with specifics instead of vague claims like 'we improve productivity.' It's a fast, practical six-minute talk aimed at founders and product marketers who keep losing rooms to jargon-heavy pitches.
key_points: Generic AI pitches built from stacked buzzwords ('agentic orchestration platform for enterprise knowledge retrieval') make listeners feel nothing and are a major reason AI products stall in the market.
The first slide should immerse the audience in their own workday and the thing they are already tired of doing, never in what the company built.
The wound-to-fix sequence should take about 20 seconds: identify the wound, say 'we fix that,' then show how.
The comprehension bar for a pitch is whether a 17-year-old could understand what you do; failing that test loses the room.
Tying a product to an already-viral story (the McDonald's AI drive-thru putting bacon on ice cream) borrows existing public understanding instead of building it from scratch.

Concrete mental images like 'Devin, the AI software engineer' or 'a smoke alarm for AI behavior' work as front doors even though they aren't precise technical definitions — the technical version comes later, to close.

Abstract value claims ('we improve code quality with AI') should be replaced with a specific before/after: 30 minutes digging through docs and tickets becomes one question answered in 10 seconds with sources attached.
Distribution has changed: building something great is no longer enough for the market to find you, and the clearest stories are what get funded, bought, and talked about.

notable_quotes.text: And in this market, that shot lasts about the time it takes to ride an elevator.
notable_quotes.why: Frames the whole talk's constraint — attention, not technology, is the scarce resource.

notable_quotes.text: What is the exact moment your user wants to throw their laptop out a window?
notable_quotes.why: The concrete diagnostic question behind the 'wound' concept.

notable_quotes.text: To demonstrate their wound, follow one rule. Do not start with what you built.
notable_quotes.why: States the single hardest rule for founders to follow, as a flat prohibition.

notable_quotes.text: The very first slide of your pitch should immerse people in their day-to-day of their job. And show them what they are already tired of doing.
notable_quotes.why: Turns the abstract advice into a checkable requirement on a specific artifact.

notable_quotes.text: The format is simple. In about 20 seconds, you need to do three things. Identify the wound, say we fix that, then show how.
notable_quotes.why: Gives the method a time budget and an explicit ordering.

notable_quotes.text: Once you've shown them the wound, your next job is to make the product click. Here's the test. Could a 17-year-old understand what you do? If not, you're probably going to lose the room.
notable_quotes.why: The talk's most portable heuristic for pitch clarity.

notable_quotes.text: One of the fastest ways to fix that is to tie your product to a viral story people already understand.
notable_quotes.why: Names the specific tactic — borrowing existing public comprehension.

notable_quotes.text: If McDonald's had used us, that drive-thru never would have made it to TikTok. We catch when AI agents go off script and give teams a chance to correct them before it becomes a PR nightmare.
notable_quotes.why: A fully worked rewrite of 'agent observability platform' into a story.

notable_quotes.text: You can give the technical version later to close the sale. Just don't make it the first thing people have to understand.
notable_quotes.why: Answers the obvious objection that simplification sacrifices accuracy, by sequencing rather than dropping it.

notable_quotes.text: A lot of founders will say things like, "We improve code quality with AI." or "We increase productivity." That sounds nice, but I still do not know what actually changes for me once your product enters my world.
notable_quotes.why: Pinpoints why generic value claims fail even when they're true.

notable_quotes.text: Before your support team spends 30 minutes digging through docs and tickets, with us, they ask one question and get the answer in 10 seconds with the sources attached.
notable_quotes.why: The one quantified before/after example in the talk.

notable_quotes.text: 15 years ago, if you built something great, the market might have found you.
notable_quotes.why: States the market-structure claim that justifies prioritizing narrative over craft.

notable_quotes.text: Identify the wound, make your product click, show the transformation, then your idea won't fail
notable_quotes.why: The three-step method compressed into one line.

positions.claim: Many AI products are failing in the market primarily because their pitches are incomprehensible, not because the technology is inadequate.
A pitch should open with the customer's pain rather than with a description of what the company built.
The wound, the fix, and the how can and should be delivered in roughly 20 seconds.
If a 17-year-old cannot understand what your product does, you will lose the room.
Imprecise but vivid descriptions are acceptable — even preferable — as an opening, because technical precision can be supplied later in the sales conversation.
Buzzword-laden category language like 'agentic AI orchestration platform' or 'agent observability platform' actively harms comprehension and should not be used to open.
Abstract benefit statements such as 'we increase productivity' fail to convey value; only a concrete before/after comparison does.
Product quality alone no longer generates market discovery the way it did roughly 15 years ago; clarity of story now determines which products get funded and bought.
Anchoring a pitch to an already-viral public incident is one of the most efficient ways to make an unfamiliar product category legible.
